This report documents the inverse-intensity (Horvitz–Thompson, Hájek) and doubly robust estimators
of a box-year mean OHC anomaly, the simulation-based estimate of the Argo sampling intensity they
require, and the full-GLORYS validation design. Results sections load their result files when they
exist. Only the 1000-replicate chain results are final.

# Setting and estimand {#sec-setting}

**Measure space.** Spacetime is $\mathcal X = \mathbb S^2\times\mathbb R$ with its Borel
$\sigma$-algebra. Let $\sigma$ be surface measure on the sphere of radius $R_\oplus$ (units m$^2$)
and $\lambda$ Lebesgue measure on time (days), and set $\mu = \sigma\otimes\lambda$ (units
m$^2\,$day). Let $M$ be the OHC mask, the union of native GLORYS $1/12^\circ$ cells with
$\mathrm{deptho}>2000$ m on which the $0$–$2000$ m integral is defined. For box
$b\in\{A,B\}$, with A $=22$–$34^\circ$N, B $=34$–$45^\circ$N, both $60$–$40^\circ$W, let $A_b$ be
the union of native cells whose centres lie in the box's closed rectangle (Box A stops at
$33.99^\circ$N so the two are disjoint). For year $y\in\{2015,\dots,2019\}$ let $T_y$ be the year
on the $365$-day calendar of the residual field. The **box-year domain** is
$\mathcal X_k = (A_b\cap M)\times T_y$ for $k=(b,y)$, and its target probability measure is the
normalized restriction
$$
\mathbb P_k(E) \;=\; \frac{\mu(E\cap\mathcal X_k)}{\mu(\mathcal X_k)},\qquad E\in\mathcal B(\mathcal X).
$$

**Field and estimand.** $Z:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ is the $0$–$2000$ m OHC residual: GLORYS OHC minus
a per-cell mean field $\Theta$ with a quadratic trend plus annual and semiannual harmonics, fitted
on 1995–2019 (`code/osim/build_residual_field.py`; see the simulation report). $Z$ is a simple
function, constant on native cell-days, so every $\mathbb P_k$-integral below is an exact finite sum.
The estimand is the linear functional
$$
\bar Z_k \;=\; \langle Z,\mathbb P_k\rangle \;=\; \int_{\mathcal X} Z\,d\mathbb P_k ,
$$
computed exactly by `ipw.box_truth` as the cell-area-and-day weighted mean on $\mathcal X_k$.
(A profile dated 29 February 2016 reads the 28 February value; $\mathbb P_k$ gives that day zero
mass. This convention affects only profiles, not the estimand.)

# The sampling intensity $q$ {#sec-intensity}

**Design space and frame.** A design outcome $\omega\in(\Omega,\mathcal F,\Pr)$ is a set of
deployments $s_j=(\text{launch position},\ \text{launch time},\ \text{lifespan})$. We work in the
**deployment-law frame**: the velocity field $u$ and the field $Z$ are fixed (conditioned upon), and
the only randomness is which deployments occur, $\{s_j\}\sim\mathcal D$. Advection is a
deterministic map $\Phi_u$ from a deployment to its profile positions, so the profile counting
measure
$$
N(E)\;=\;\sum_i \delta_{x_i}(E),\qquad \{x_i\}=\textstyle\bigcup_j \Phi_u(s_j),
$$
is a random, locally finite counting measure on $\mathcal X$. Its **intensity measure** is
$\Lambda(E)=\mathbb E[N(E)]$. Assume $\Lambda$ is $\sigma$-finite and $\Lambda\ll\mu$; the
**sampling intensity** is the Radon–Nikodym derivative
$$
q \;=\; \frac{d\Lambda}{d\mu}\qquad(\text{profiles m}^{-2}\,\text{day}^{-1}),
$$
defined $\mu$-a.e. and a functional of $(\mathcal D,u)$ only.

**Campbell's theorem** [@daley2003]. For every measurable $f\ge 0$, or $f\in L^1(\Lambda)$,
$$
\mathbb E\Big[\sum_i f(x_i)\Big] \;=\; \int_{\mathcal X} f\,d\Lambda \;=\; \int_{\mathcal X} f\,q\,d\mu .
\tag{2.1}
$$
$f$ must be fixed with respect to the design (not a function of $\omega$); this requirement recurs
in @sec-aipw. Taking $f = Z\,\mathbf 1_{\mathcal X_k}/(q\,\mu(\mathcal X_k))$ gives the continuous
Horvitz–Thompson theorem [@horvitz1952; @cordy1993]:
$$
\mathbb E\Big[\frac{1}{\mu(\mathcal X_k)}\sum_{x_i\in\mathcal X_k}\frac{Z(x_i)}{q(x_i)}\Big]
\;=\; \int_{\mathcal X_k\cap\{q>0\}} Z\,d\mathbb P_k
\;=\; \bar Z_k \;-\; \int_{\mathcal X_k\cap\{q=0\}} Z\,d\mathbb P_k .
\tag{2.2}
$$
The remainder vanishes iff $\mathbb P_k(\{q=0\}\cap\{Z\neq 0\})=0$; the design-level sufficient
condition is **positivity**, $\mathbb P_k\ll\Lambda$.

## $q$ versus the estimator density $w$ {#sec-q-vs-w}

For a linear estimator $\hat Z=\sum_i a_iZ(x_i)$ with estimator measure $\nu=\sum_i a_i\delta_{x_i}$
(restricted to $\mathcal X_k$), let $\mathbb E[\nu]$ be its mean measure,
$\int f\,d\mathbb E[\nu]=\mathbb E\sum_i a_if(x_i)$ for bounded measurable $f$, and, when
$\mathbb E[\nu]\ll\mathbb P_k$,
$$
w \;=\; \frac{d\,\mathbb E[\nu]}{d\mathbb P_k},\qquad m \;=\; \int w\,d\mathbb P_k \;=\; \mathbb E[\nu(\mathcal X_k)] .
$$
The two densities answer different questions:

* $q=d\Lambda/d\mu$ is a property of the **design alone**: the unweighted counting measure against the
  unnormalized $\mu$ (profiles m$^{-2}$ day$^{-1}$; $\int_{\mathcal X_k}q\,d\mu=\mathbb E[n_k]$).
* $w$ is a property of **design and estimator**: it carries the weights $a_i$, is dimensionless, and
  enters the bias. For every linear estimator the realized bias is exact and density-free,
  $B=\hat Z-\bar Z_k=\langle Z,\nu-\mathbb P_k\rangle$, and, where $w$ exists,
$$
\mathbb E[B] \;=\; \int Z\,(w-1)\,d\mathbb P_k \;=\; \operatorname{Cov}_{\mathbb P_k}(w,Z)+(m-1)\,\bar Z_k .
\tag{2.3}
$$

**Link for position-only weights.** Suppose $a_i=a(x_i)$ for a fixed measurable $a\ge0$ on
$\mathcal X_k$. Since $\mathbb P_k=\mu|_{\mathcal X_k}/\mu(\mathcal X_k)$, Campbell's theorem (2.1)
gives, for bounded measurable $f$,
$$
\int f\,d\mathbb E[\nu] \;=\; \mathbb E\sum_{x_i\in\mathcal X_k}a(x_i)f(x_i) \;=\; \int_{\mathcal X_k} f\,a\,q\,d\mu
\;=\; \int f\,\big(a\,q\,\mu(\mathcal X_k)\big)\,d\mathbb P_k ,
$$
so, by uniqueness of the Radon–Nikodym derivative,
$$
w \;=\; a\,q\,\mu(\mathcal X_k)\quad\mathbb P_k\text{-a.e.},\qquad m=\int_{\mathcal X_k}a\,q\,d\mu .
\tag{2.4}
$$
Choosing $a$ to make $w\equiv1$ is exactly inverse-intensity weighting.

**Cases.**

1. *Horvitz–Thompson, true $q$:* $a=\mathbf 1_{\{q>0\}}/(q\,\mu(\mathcal X_k))$. By (2.4)
   $w=\mathbf 1_{\{q>0\}}$ and $m=\mathbb P_k(q>0)$, and (2.3) reduces to the positivity remainder of
   (2.2), $\mathbb E[B]=-\int_{\{q=0\}}Z\,d\mathbb P_k$.
2. *Horvitz–Thompson, estimated $\hat q$* (fixed with respect to the design, e.g. built from
   independent replicates): $a=\mathbf 1_{\{\hat q>0\}}/(\hat q\,\mu(\mathcal X_k))$ gives
   $w=(q/\hat q)\,\mathbf 1_{\{\hat q>0\}}$ and
   $$
   \mathbb E[B]\;=\;\int Z\Big(\frac{q}{\hat q}-1\Big)d\mathbb P_k
   \;=\;\operatorname{Cov}_{\mathbb P_k}\!\Big(\frac{q}{\hat q},Z\Big)+(m-1)\,\bar Z_k ,
   \qquad m=\int\frac{q}{\hat q}\,d\mathbb P_k ,
   $$
   so a scale error in $\hat q$ enters through $m\ne1$.
3. *Hájek.* The weights $a_i=v_i/\sum_jv_j$, $v=1/\hat q$, depend on the whole configuration, so (2.4)
   does not apply. Writing $\hat Z_H=A/D$ with $A=\sum_iv_iZ(x_i)$ and $D=\sum_iv_i$, (2.1) gives
   $\mathbb E[A]=\mu(\mathcal X_k)\int Z\,q/\hat q\,d\mathbb P_k$ and
   $\mathbb E[D]=\mu(\mathcal X_k)\,m$, and the standard ratio expansion yields
   $$
   \mathbb E[\hat Z_H]-\bar Z_k \;=\; \frac{\operatorname{Cov}_{\mathbb P_k}(q/\hat q,\,Z)}{m}
   \;+\;R_H,\qquad R_H=\frac{\mathbb E[A]\operatorname{Var}D/\mathbb E[D]-\operatorname{Cov}(A,D)}{\mathbb E[D]^2}+o(\cdot),
   $$
   with $R_H$ of order $1/n_{\mathrm{eff}}$. The scale of $\hat q$ cancels: only the shape of
   $q/\hat q$ matters.
4. *Simple mean:* $a_i=\mathbf 1_{\{n_k\ge1\}}/n_k$ depends on the configuration through $n_k$, so
   $\mathbb E[\nu](E)=\mathbb E[N(E)/n_k;\,n_k\ge1]$. If, given $n_k=n$, the $n$ in-box locations were
   i.i.d. with density $q/\Lambda(\mathcal X_k)$ with respect to $\mu$ (a mixed binomial process),
   then $\mathbb E[N(E)/n\mid n_k=n]=\Lambda(E)/\Lambda(\mathcal X_k)$ and
   $$
   w \;=\; \Pr(n_k\ge1)\,\frac{q}{\bar q_k}\;+\;r_k,\qquad \bar q_k=\frac{\Lambda(\mathcal X_k)}{\mu(\mathcal X_k)},
   $$
   with $r_k\equiv0$. For advected floats the location law depends on $n_k$ (profiles cluster along
   tracks, and configurations with more in-box floats are spatially different), so
   $r_k=d\,\mathbb E[\nu]/d\mathbb P_k-\Pr(n_k\ge1)\,q/\bar q_k\neq0$ in general. To this order, the
   simple mean's $w$ is $q$ normalized to $\mathbb P_k$-mean one, and its bias is
   $\operatorname{Cov}_{\mathbb P_k}(q/\bar q_k,Z)$ up to $r_k$ and $\Pr(n_k=0)$.
5. *Kriging (KS):* $a_i=\sum_g c_g\alpha_i(x_g^*)$ depends on all locations through $K^{-1}$ (and on
   fitted covariance parameters), so $w$ is not a functional of $q$; it is the declustered
   occupancy, estimable only as the ensemble mean of $\nu$.

**Notation.** In the simulation report (and `outlines/paper_outline.md`, §2.2) the symbol $q$ denotes
the normalized occupancy of the simple mean, $d\,\mathbb E[\nu]/d\mathbb P$ with $a_i=1/n$; by case 4
that object is a $w$ here, $\approx q/\bar q_k$. Throughout this report $q$ is the intensity and $w$
the estimator density.

# Deployment law and GLORYS simulation {#sec-deploy}

Code: `code/osim/continuous_sim.py` (`write_resample_pool`, `resample_seeds`, `_main_resample`,
`run_continuous`, `profiles_from_tracks`) and `code/osim/argo_meta.py`.

**Pool.** Every float in `data/argo_ohc.csv` launched inside the velocity domain
($11.25$–$65.75^\circ$N, $86.75$–$12.25^\circ$W), in water at least as deep as the $1000$ m park
depth, between 2010-01-01 and 2019-12-26: $994$ launches. The launch position and time are those of
the GDAC `_meta.nc` (`LAUNCH_LATITUDE`, `LAUNCH_LONGITUDE`, `LAUNCH_DATE`) when consistent with the
float's first profile, meaning the launch is no more than $1$ day after that profile and within
$50+20\max(\Delta t,0)$ km of it for $\Delta t$ days elapsed; otherwise the first profile is used.
$964$ launches come from metadata and $30$ are fallbacks. Six shallow-water launches were
excluded. There is no float-level QC.

**Lifespan.** $L_j$ is operating life, from launch to the last profile of any depth, and travels with
the deployment.

**Deployment law $\hat{\mathcal D}$.** A year-stratified smoothed bootstrap. With $\mathcal P_y$ the
pool entries launched in year $y$ and $N_y=|\mathcal P_y|$, a replicate draws $N_y$ entries i.i.d.
uniformly from $\mathcal P_y$ with replacement, for each $y$, carrying position, date and lifespan
jointly. Each draw is jittered by independent $U_1,U_2\sim\mathrm{Unif}(-h,h)$, $h=1/12^\circ$, as
$(\varphi+U_1,\ \ell+U_2/\cos\varphi)$ (a square of half-width $h$ of arc in a local isometric
chart), and $U_3\sim\mathrm{Unif}(-10,10)$ days in time. A jittered position off deep water is
redrawn (at most $50$ times, then left unjittered), positions are clipped to the velocity domain,
and release times to the advection window. The lifespan is not jittered.

Equivalently, one draw from year $y$ has law equal to the empirical deployment measure of
$\mathcal P_y$ convolved with a uniform kernel, where rejection truncates each point's kernel to deep
water and renormalizes it. The jitter is a smoothing bandwidth that gives $\hat{\mathcal D}$, and
hence $\Lambda$, a density; it is not a model of trajectory error. Fixing $N_y$ conditions on the
programmatic deployment rate.

**Ramp-up.** Deployments in 2010–2014 are ramp-up and the analysis years are 2015–2019. No real
in-box profile after 2014 comes from a float launched before 2010, so no initial-state floats are
seeded.

**Advection.** OceanParcels, `AdvectionRK4`, $1$ h step, at the $1000$ m park depth. GLORYS12
daily $(u,v)$ is pre-interpolated to $1000$ m, which is exact up to float32 rounding because
Parcels zeroes NaN and interpolates linearly in depth. A float is deleted when its age exceeds $L_j$
or when it leaves the velocity domain. Positions are recorded daily; nominal $10$-day profiles are
placed at release $+\,10k$ days, $k\ge1$, up to the last recorded position, by linear
interpolation in $(\varphi,\ell)$ between daily positions. There are $R=1000$ independent
replicates. Under $\hat{\mathcal D}$ the flow is fixed and the draws are i.i.d. within each year,
so **simulated float trajectories are mutually independent**; @sec-aipw relies on this.

**Eligibility and the thinning theorem.** The real profiles used by any estimator are *eligible*:
duplicates less than $2$ days apart are removed by greedy per-float thinning, then
$\text{max\_depth}\ge1900$ m is required (`intensity.eligible`). For source float $k$ and yearly age
bin $a=[365.25\,j,\,365.25\,(j+1))$, the eligible-profile rate is
$$
\rho_k(a) \;=\; \frac{\#\{\text{eligible real profiles of }k\text{ with age in }a\}}
{\lfloor |a\cap[0,L_k]|/10\rfloor}\,,
$$
the number of eligible profiles per nominal cycle (`intensity.eligibility_rates`). A simulated
float resampled from $k$ carries $\rho_k$, and its profile of age $a_i$ carries the mark
$\rho_{k_i}(a_i)$. **Assumption:** given the source float and age bin, the expected number of
eligible profiles per nominal cycle is $\rho_k(a)$ whatever the cycle's position. Under it, the
Campbell theorem for marked processes gives the eligible-profile intensity measure
$$
\Lambda^{e}(E) \;=\; \mathbb E\Big[\sum_i \rho_{k_i}(a_i)\,\delta_{x_i}(E)\Big],
\qquad q^{e} = d\Lambda^{e}/d\mu .
$$
When $\rho\le1$ this is independent $\rho$-thinning. $\rho$ can exceed $1$ for floats cycling
faster than $10$ days, in which case it is a rate-weighted mark rather than a retention probability,
and the identity still holds. $q^{e}$ weights **real** positions. Simulated nominal profiles are
their own design, so the GLORYS chain (@sec-results) uses the nominal intensity $q$, with mark $1$.

# Estimating $q$ from the replicates {#sec-qhat}

Code: `code/osim/intensity.py` (`eligibility_rates`, `native_grid`, `binned_counts`,
`fine_support`, `smooth`, `build_kernel`, `at`). The grid version is `build`.

**Binned counts.** The cells $c$ are the native GLORYS $1/12^\circ$ cells (edges at the midpoints
of the model's cell centres) times calendar days, covering $20$–$48^\circ$N, $62$–$38^\circ$W,
2014-10-01 to 2020-01-01. They form the partition on which $Z$ is constant. Then
$$
C(c) \;=\; \frac1R\sum_{r=1}^R\sum_{p\in N_r} w_p\,\mathbf 1_c(x_p),\qquad w_p\in\{1,\ \rho_{k_p}(a_p)\}.
$$
The replicates are i.i.d., so by (2.1) $\mathbb E[C(c)] = \Lambda^{(w)}(c)$ exactly.

**Support measure.** The float support is
$\mathcal S=\{\mathrm{deptho}\ge1000\text{ m}\}\cap(\text{velocity domain})\times(\text{advection window})$,
and $\Lambda$ is carried by $\mathcal S$. The bathymetry is defined per native cell, so $\mathcal S$
is a union of cells $c$, and `fine_support` computes $\mu(c\cap\mathcal S)$ exactly: the spherical
area $R_\oplus^2\,\Delta\ell\,(\sin\varphi_2-\sin\varphi_1)$ of the cell, times the days of $c$
inside the window.

**Kernel estimator.** With $G$ a separable Gaussian on the grid index, standard deviations
$\sigma_s/(1/12^\circ)$ cells in both latitude and longitude and $\sigma_t/(1\text{ d})$ cells in time,
truncated at $4$ standard deviations and zero outside the grid,
$$
\hat q(c) \;=\; \frac{(G*C)(c)}{(G*\mu_{\mathcal S})(c)},\qquad \mu_{\mathcal S}(c)=\mu(c\cap\mathcal S),
$$
left undefined where $\mu_{\mathcal S}(c)=0$. This is the binned form of Diggle's edge-corrected
kernel intensity estimator [@diggle1985],
$\hat q(x)=\sum_i k(x-x_i)/\int_{\mathcal S}k(x-y)\,\mu(dy)$. The denominator is the kernel mass
inside the support, so the estimator is not biased downward at coasts, the domain edge or the end of
the record. Non-uniform cell areas enter through $\mu_{\mathcal S}$. The kernel is isotropic in
degrees, so in physical distance its zonal width is $\sigma_s\cos\varphi$ of arc.

Binning is a computational device. It is exact in the denominator, and in the numerator it moves
each profile to its cell-day. *Heuristic:* if positions are roughly uniform within a cell-day,
binning acts in expectation like an extra uniform kernel of one cell width $\delta$. The effective
bandwidth is then $(\sigma^2+\delta^2/12)^{1/2}$, which at the bandwidth below is $1\%$ above
$\sigma_s$ and $0.3\%$ above $\sigma_t$.

**Bandwidth.** The bandwidth is fixed a priori at $\sigma_s=1/6^\circ$ (two native cells, about
$17$ km) and $\sigma_t=4$ d. There is no data-driven selection. Four considerations fix it:

1. *Variance.* Pooled over $R=1000$, the mean count in the boxes is about $0.10$ profiles per native
   cell-day. A separable Gaussian's effective volume is $(2\sqrt\pi)^3\sigma_x\sigma_y\sigma_t$ in
   cell units, so the kernel holds about $70$ expected counts at the mean intensity. That gives a
   relative Monte Carlo sd of about $12\%$ and a Jensen term in (4.1) of about $1.4\%$. This
   heuristic assumes $\kappa_h\approx1$, and both figures grow where $q$ is below its mean.
2. *Bias.* The fitted exponential covariance of $Z$ in the boxes has ranges of $1.5$–$3.9^\circ$
   zonally, $1.0$–$3.2^\circ$ meridionally and $25$–$117$ d in time. For an exponential covariance
   the share of $\operatorname{Var}Z$ at lags below $h$ is about $h/\theta$. So the part of $Z$
   that can covary with sub-bandwidth structure of $q$, which the kernel smooths away, is a small
   fraction. Eddy-scale trapping (radii near $50$ km), the preferential mechanism of interest, is
   resolved.
3. *Advective coupling.* $\sigma_t\approx\sigma_s/U$ with a park-depth speed $U\approx3$–$4$ km/d.
4. *Floor.* The flow and $Z$ are defined on native cell-days, and GLORYS's effective resolution is
   several cells, so there is no gain below one cell or one day.

**Error decomposition.** The denominator is deterministic, so $\mathbb E[\hat q] = \bar q_h :=
(G*\Lambda)/(G*\mu_{\mathcal S})$ exactly, and
$$
\hat q - q \;=\; \underbrace{(\bar q_h - q)}_{\text{smoothing bias}} \;+\; \underbrace{(\hat q-\bar q_h)}_{\text{Monte Carlo error}} .
$$
For $q\in C^2$ the smoothing bias is $O(h^2)$ in the interior and $O(h)$ within a bandwidth of
$\partial\mathcal S$. The Monte Carlo variance is
$\operatorname{Var}\hat q = O\big(\kappa_h\,q/(R\,h_s^2h_t)\big)$, where $\kappa_h\ge1$ is the
over-dispersion from consecutive profiles of one float falling inside one kernel (along-track
clustering). The estimators use $1/\hat q$, which is nonlinear. With $\delta=(\hat q-q)/q$ the
identity $q/\hat q = 1-\delta+\delta^2\,q/\hat q$ is exact, so
$$
\mathbb E\!\left[\frac{q}{\hat q}\right]-1 \;=\; -\frac{\bar q_h-q}{q} \;+\; \mathbb E\!\left[\delta^2\frac{q}{\hat q}\right],
\tag{4.1}
$$
where the second term is a nonnegative Jensen effect of order $\operatorname{Var}(\hat q)/q^2 =
O\big((R\,h_s^2h_t)^{-1}\big)$. With $h_s\propto h_t\propto h$, the MSE-optimal bandwidth for $\hat q$
balances $h^4$ against $(Rh^3)^{-1}$, so $h\propto R^{-1/7}$ in three dimensions. Balancing the two
*signed* first-order terms of (4.1) instead gives $h\propto R^{-1/5}$. Both rates are heuristics:
the estimators integrate (4.1) against a residual (§5), and the two terms can cancel there. A
coarse histogram estimator ($2^\circ\times2$ months, `intensity.build`) was tried first and left
substantial bias. Its piecewise-constant bias is $O(h)$ at a bin width comparable to the gyre-scale
gradients of $q$, which motivates the fine kernel estimator.

**In-sample weighting (approximation).** For real positions the simulated $\hat q$ is independent
of the real design by construction. In the GLORYS chain, every replicate is weighted by the same
$\hat q$ built from all $R$ replicates, including its own. Replicate $r$ then contributes
$G*C_r/R$ to the numerator at exactly its own profile positions. Relative to the pooled count that
contribution is of order $(R\,q\,V_h)^{-1}$, where $V_h$ is the kernel's effective volume: about
$1$–$3\%$ at the mean intensity once a float's own neighbouring cycles are counted, and larger
where $q$ is low. It is not of order $1/R$, because it is concentrated at the evaluation points.
Condition (2.1), that $\hat q$ be fixed with respect to the weighted design, therefore holds only
approximately. @tbl-insample measures the effect by re-weighting $50$ replicates with $\hat q$
built from the other $950$.

**Lookup.** $v_i=1/\hat q(c(x_i))$ is the value in the containing native cell-day
(`intensity.at`), the same cell-day on which $Z$ is read. Profiles where $\hat q=0$ or $\hat q$ is
undefined get no finite weight and are dropped (reported as `missing`). The estimators then target
$\mathcal X_k\cap\{\hat q>0\}$, and a remainder like that of (2.2) applies.

**Box membership.** A profile belongs to box $b$ if and only if the centre of its containing
native cell lies in the box's rectangle. This is the definition of $A_b$ in @sec-setting.

# Estimators {#sec-estimators}

Code: `code/osim/ipw.py` (`estimate`, `predict_points`, `folds`) and `code/osim/krige_estimate.py`
(`aggregated_weights`, `prediction_grid`). Write $I_k=\{i:x_i\in\mathcal X_k\}$, $n_k=|I_k|$,
$Z_i=Z(x_i)$ and $v_i=1/\hat q(x_i)$. Each estimator is linear in $Z$ given its weights and is
listed with its estimator measure $\nu$.

## Naive, Horvitz–Thompson, Hájek

$$
\hat Z_{\mathrm{naive}}=\frac1{n_k}\sum_{i\in I_k}Z_i,\qquad
\hat Z_{\mathrm{HT}}=\frac{1}{\mu(\mathcal X_k)}\sum_{i\in I_k}v_iZ_i,\qquad
\hat Z_{\mathrm H}=\frac{\sum_{i\in I_k}v_iZ_i}{\sum_{i\in I_k}v_i}
$$
[@horvitz1952; @hajek1971]. Conditional on a design-independent $\hat q$, (2.1) gives
$\mathbb E[\hat Z_{\mathrm{HT}}\mid\hat q]=\int Z\,\lambda\,d\mathbb P_k$ with
$\lambda=q/\hat q$, so
$$
\mathbb E[B_{\mathrm{HT}}\mid\hat q] \;=\; \int_{\mathcal X_k} Z\,(\lambda-1)\,d\mathbb P_k,
\qquad m_{\mathrm{HT}}=\int\lambda\,d\mathbb P_k .
$$
$\nu_{\mathrm H}=\sum v_i\delta_{x_i}/\sum v_i$ has unit mass in every realization, so
$B_{\mathrm H}=\langle Z-\bar Z_k,\nu_{\mathrm H}-\mathbb P_k\rangle$ and $\hat Z_{\mathrm H}$ is
invariant to $\hat q\mapsto c\,\hat q$. Write $\hat Z_{\mathrm H}=\hat A/\hat D$ with
$\hat A=\hat Z_{\mathrm{HT}}$ and $\hat D=\mu(\mathcal X_k)^{-1}\sum v_i$, let
$A=\mathbb E[\hat A\mid\hat q]$ and $D=\mathbb E[\hat D\mid\hat q]=m_{\mathrm{HT}}$, and set
$r=A/D$. The exact identity
$$
\hat Z_{\mathrm H}-r \;=\; D^{-1}(\hat A-r\hat D) \;-\; D^{-1}(\hat D-D)(\hat Z_{\mathrm H}-r)
$$
has a mean-zero first term, so
$\mathbb E[\hat Z_{\mathrm H}\mid\hat q]-r=-D^{-1}\mathbb E[(\hat D-D)(\hat Z_{\mathrm H}-r)\mid\hat q]$.
This ratio remainder is $O(1/n_k)$ under standard moment conditions (larger, $O(1/n_{\mathrm{eff}})$,
under along-track clustering). The population target of the Hájek estimator is
$r=\int Z\lambda\,d\mathbb P_k/\int\lambda\,d\mathbb P_k$, which equals $\bar Z_k$ whenever
$\lambda$ is constant on $\mathcal X_k$.

## Kuusela–Stein simple kriging

The simple-kriging map $\hat m(x)=\sum_j\alpha_j(x)Z_j$ uses the oracle locally stationary
anisotropic exponential covariance fitted on the complete GLORYS field [@kuusela2018]. Parameters
come from the containing $2^\circ$ parameter cell, with nugget ratio floored at $10^{-6}$, and $j$
runs over profiles within $\pm10^\circ$ and $\pm180$ d of the block centre. The box-year integral is
approximated on the $1^\circ\times$month grid $\{x^*_g\}$ with weights $c_g$ equal to the exact
$\mathbb P_k$-mass of each cell-month:
$$
\hat Z_{\mathrm{KS}}=\sum_g c_g\,\hat m(x^*_g)=\sum_j a_jZ_j,\qquad a_j=\sum_g c_g\alpha_j(x^*_g),
\qquad \nu_{\mathrm{KS}}=\sum_j a_j\delta_{x_j},
$$
with mass $m=\sum_ja_j$. Simple kriging reverts to its zero prior mean where under-informed, so
typically $m\le1$ (not a theorem for simple kriging, where screening can push $\sum_j\alpha_j$ above
one). The quadrature remainder
$R^{\mathrm{quad}}=\sum_g c_g\hat m(x^*_g)-\int\hat m\,d\mathbb P_k$ is carried explicitly. Because
$\nu_{\mathrm{KS}}$ puts mass outside $\mathcal X_k$, $\mathbb E[\nu_{\mathrm{KS}}]\not\ll\mathbb P_k$,
and only the density-free identity $B=\langle Z,\nu_{\mathrm{KS}}-\mathbb P_k\rangle$ applies.

## Augmented IPW / doubly robust estimator {#sec-aipw}

Floats are split into $K=5$ folds by a random permutation of float ids (`ipw.folds`); fold labels
are independent of trajectories. For fold $k$, $\hat m_{-k}$ is the kriging map conditioned on all
profiles *not* in fold $k$. It is evaluated at held-out points by `predict_points`, which uses the
same (parameter cell, month) conditioning blocks as the grid, so $\hat m_{-k}$ is one function.
With $I^{(k)}$ the fold-$k$ profiles in $\mathcal X_k$ that have finite $v_i$, the DML1 estimator
[@chernozhukov2018] is
$$
\hat Z_{\mathrm{DR}}=\frac1{K'}\sum_{k}\hat\theta_k,\qquad
\hat\theta_k=\sum_g c_g\hat m_{-k}(x^*_g)+\frac{\sum_{i\in I^{(k)}}v_i\,(Z_i-\hat m_{-k}(x_i))}{\sum_{i\in I^{(k)}}v_i},
$$
over the $K'\le K$ folds with $I^{(k)}\neq\varnothing$.

**Realized identity (exact).** Let $\nu_{\mathrm H,k}=\sum_{i\in I^{(k)}}v_i\delta_{x_i}/\sum_{i\in I^{(k)}}v_i$.
Adding and subtracting $\int\hat m_{-k}\,d\mathbb P_k$ gives, for every realization, every
$\hat q$ and every $\hat m$,
$$
\hat\theta_k-\bar Z_k \;=\; \big\langle Z-\hat m_{-k},\ \nu_{\mathrm H,k}-\mathbb P_k\big\rangle \;+\; R^{\mathrm{quad}}_k,
\qquad
B_{\mathrm{DR}}=\frac1{K'}\sum_k\Big[\big\langle Z-\hat m_{-k},\nu_{\mathrm H,k}-\mathbb P_k\big\rangle+R^{\mathrm{quad}}_k\Big].
\tag{5.1}
$$
This is pure algebra. Averaging per-fold estimates (DML1) keeps it exact because each fold pairs its
own unit-mass $\nu_{\mathrm H,k}$ with its own $\int\hat m_{-k}\,d\mathbb P_k$. Pooling the corrections
under one normalization (DML2) instead gives fold $k$ the mass
$\hat\pi_k=\sum_{I^{(k)}}v_i/\sum_{\cup I^{(k)}}v_i$ and leaves a mismatch
$\sum_k(\hat\pi_k-1/K')\int\hat m_{-k}\,d\mathbb P_k$.

**Expected identity.** Let $\mathcal G_{-k}$ be the $\sigma$-field of $\hat q$, the fold labels and
the design outside fold $k$, so that $\hat m_{-k}$ is $\mathcal G_{-k}$-measurable. Let
$\Lambda_{k\mid-k}(E)=\mathbb E[N_k(E)\mid\mathcal G_{-k}]$ with density $q_{k\mid-k}$, let
$\Lambda_k=\mathbb E[N_k]$ with density $q_k$, and let $\hat q_k$ be $\hat q$ rescaled to fold $k$
(for the Hájek form the scale cancels). Applying (2.1) conditionally, with the $\mathcal G_{-k}$-fixed
test function $g=(Z-\hat m_{-k})\mathbf 1_{\mathcal X_k}/\hat q_k$, to the Horvitz–Thompson form of the
correction gives
$$
\mathbb E[\tilde\theta_k-\bar Z_k\mid\mathcal G_{-k}]
=\int_{\mathcal X_k}(Z-\hat m_{-k})\Big(\frac{q_k}{\hat q_k}-1\Big)d\mathbb P_k
\;+\;\underbrace{\int_{\mathcal X_k}(Z-\hat m_{-k})\frac{q_{k\mid-k}-q_k}{\hat q_k}\,d\mathbb P_k}_{R^{\mathrm{dep}}_k}
\;+\;R^{\mathrm{quad}}_k ,
\tag{5.2}
$$
and the Hájek form adds the ratio remainder above. Up to normalization, (5.2) is
$\mathbb E[B]=\int(Z-\hat m)(q/\hat q-1)\,d\mu$ plus remainders. It needs a test function fixed with
respect to the fold-$k$ design; cross-fitting supplies this only insofar as $R^{\mathrm{dep}}_k=0$,
that is, only if fold-$k$ floats are independent of the others given $\mathcal G_{-k}$.

* In the **GLORYS chain** this holds exactly: under $\hat{\mathcal D}$ the trajectories are i.i.d.
  within year and independent across years, and the labels are independent of them, so
  $R^{\mathrm{dep}}_k=0$.
* For the **real array** it is an approximation. Floats share deployment cruises (co-located,
  co-timed launches under the true $\mathcal D$), and in any frame where the flow is random they
  share the flow too. Then $R^{\mathrm{dep}}_k\neq0$. Cross-fitting by independent deployment
  cluster would restore it, in the spirit of multiway cluster DML [@chiang2022].

**Cauchy–Schwarz ceiling.** From the leading term of (5.2),
$$
\Big|\int(Z-\hat m_{-k})\Big(\frac{q_k}{\hat q_k}-1\Big)d\mathbb P_k\Big|
\;\le\;\big\|Z-\hat m_{-k}\big\|_{L^2(\mathbb P_k)}\;\Big\|\frac{q_k}{\hat q_k}-1\Big\|_{L^2(\mathbb P_k)} ,
$$
a deterministic product bound. The bias vanishes if either the outcome model or the intensity is
right (double robustness), and it is second order when both errors are small.

**Relation to AIPW, GREG and DML.** $\hat\theta_k$ is the augmented IPW estimator
[@robins1994] with outcome regression $\hat m$ and "propensity" $\hat q$. It is also the
model-assisted difference (GREG-type) estimator of survey sampling [@sarndal1992], transplanted to a
continuous universe with a point-process design. The DML rate guarantee [@chernozhukov2018] does not
transfer, for two reasons:

1. $\hat q$ comes from simulation, not from the sample. Its error is governed by $R$, $h$ and the
   fidelity of $(\hat{\mathcal D},u)$, and does not vanish as $n_k$ grows.
2. The data are one realization of a dependent point process, not i.i.d. units, so there is no
   $\sqrt n$ normal limit to appeal to.

What survives is the exact identity (5.1) and the product structure of the bias.

## Residual bias and $\Gamma$-sensitivity (planned; not implemented)

The residual intensity error $\lambda=q/\hat q$ is not identified from the data. A marginal
sensitivity model in the sense of @tan2006 and @zhao2019 assumes
$\lambda(x)\in[\Gamma^{-1},\Gamma]$ on $\mathcal X_k$. For the Hájek correction term, the bounds
are
$$
\min_{h_i\in[\Gamma^{-1},\Gamma]}\ \Big/\ \max_{h_i\in[\Gamma^{-1},\Gamma]}\ \ \frac{\sum_i h_iv_ie_i}{\sum_i h_iv_i},
\qquad e_i=Z_i-\hat m_{-k}(x_i),
$$
a linear-fractional program. Its optimum takes $h_i\in\{\Gamma^{-1},\Gamma\}$ with a threshold in
the sorted $e_i$, so it is solved in $O(n\log n)$ by sorting. The resulting interval is
deterministic, a worst case over $\lambda$ in the band. $\Gamma$ is meant to absorb the departure of
real trajectories from GLORYS advection, misspecification of $\hat{\mathcal D}$, violations of the
eligibility assumption, and residual smoothing error.

# Assumptions {#sec-assumptions}

1. **Deployment-law frame.** $u$ and $Z$ are fixed; expectations are over $\mathcal D$ only (§2).
2. **Sequential ignorability.** Deployment decisions are independent of $Z$ given what $\mathcal D$
   conditions on, so $Z$ may serve as a fixed test function in (2.1).
3. **Positivity.** $\mathbb P_k\ll\Lambda$, and in practice $\hat q>0$ on $\mathcal X_k$; otherwise
   the remainder in (2.2) applies.
4. **Eligibility.** Retention (the eligible-profile rate) is independent of position given the
   source float and age bin (§3).
5. **GLORYS flow as the intensity model.** $q$ is computed under GLORYS park-depth advection. The
   real-flow departure is not modelled and belongs in the $\Gamma$ band.
6. **Unbiased measurement.** $Z$ is observed without bias at $x_i$. In the chain it is exact.
7. **Fixed climatology.** $\Theta$ is fixed (fitted once, 1995–2019), so $Z$ is not design-dependent.
8. **Float independence for cross-fitting.** Needed for $R^{\mathrm{dep}}_k=0$: exact under
   $\hat{\mathcal D}$, approximate for real Argo.

# Relation to prior work {#sec-prior}

@diggle2010 give the canonical continuous formulation of preferential sampling and a model-based
remedy through a shared latent field. The estimators here are design-based: they weight a linear
functional by an intensity obtained from a mechanistic simulation of the design. The closest
precedent is @hsiao2026, who use inverse sampling-intensity weights for preferential sampling. They
differ in four ways:

1. They weight a (Vecchia) likelihood for covariance parameters and prediction, not a linear
   functional.
2. Their intensity is estimated from the same observed locations; ours comes from an independent
   simulation of the design.
3. There is no doubly robust augmentation.
4. The setting is static and two-dimensional, not spatiotemporal.

Inverse-intensity weighting of point patterns goes back to @baddeley2000, and the Horvitz–Thompson
theorem for a continuous universe to @cordy1993. @baugh2022 frame OHC as a linear functional of a
spatial field with a Gaussian-process posterior. Our target is the same kind of functional, but the
question is the bias induced by the design rather than posterior uncertainty.

# Validation design and results {#sec-results}

**Full GLORYS chain.** The positions are one simulated replicate's nominal profiles (GLORYS
advection under $\hat{\mathcal D}$), the values are the GLORYS residual $Z$ at those positions, and
the weights are $1/\hat q$ from all $R=1000$ replicates, in-sample (@sec-qhat). Truth is $\bar Z_k$
(`ipw.box_truth`). For the union $A\cup B$ the two boxes are disjoint, so
$\bar Z_{A\cup B}=(\mu(\mathcal X_A)\bar Z_A+\mu(\mathcal X_B)\bar Z_B)/(\mu(\mathcal X_A)+\mu(\mathcal X_B))$. The
Horvitz–Thompson estimator divides by $\mu(\mathcal X_A)+\mu(\mathcal X_B)$, and the naive and Hájek
estimators pool the profiles of both boxes.
In the chain, assumptions 1, 2, 5, 6, 7 and 8 of @sec-assumptions hold by construction, 4 is moot
(nominal profiles), and positivity (3) is monitored through the `missing` count. The chain therefore
isolates the error from estimating $q$ (smoothing, Monte Carlo and Jensen, (4.1)) and, for
the doubly robust estimator, the outcome-model error.

**Result.** The naive mean is biased low in Box B in every year, by $-0.23$ to $-0.42$ GJ m$^{-2}$
($|t|>18$). In Box A its bias changes sign across years ($+0.06$ in 2016, $-0.14$ in 2018). Pooled
over 2015–2019, Hájek removes $89\%$ of the naive bias in Box B (95% CI $86$–$92$), $81\%$ in
Box A ($72$–$93$) and $89\%$ in $A\cup B$ ($87$–$92$). Horvitz–Thompson removes $86\%$, $46\%$ and
$82\%$ respectively. The gap is the scale term $(m-1)\bar Z_k$ of case 2 in @sec-q-vs-w, which
Hájek cancels. The realized mass $\sum_iv_i/\mu(\mathcal X_k)$ is $0.92$–$0.96$ in every box-year,
so the HT bias exceeds the Hájek bias by about $-0.07\,\bar Z_k$. It is largest where $\bar Z_k$ is
large: Box A, where $\bar Z_k\approx0.4$ GJ m$^{-2}$ in 2015–2017, and A $\cup$ B in 2018, where
$\bar Z_k=0.52$. In A $\cup$ B in 2018, HT therefore removes nothing. The naive bias there is also
small ($-0.04$), even though both boxes are biased low, because the pooled mean over-weights Box B
relative to its area and $\bar Z_B=1.15\gg\bar Z_A$. That composition term offsets the within-box
biases. A residual Hájek bias remains in
Box B of $-0.03$ to $-0.05$ GJ m$^{-2}$ ($|t|$ between $2.3$ and $4.1$), about $10\%$ of the naive
bias, and the same sign in every year. It is what the smoothing, Jensen and in-sample errors of
$\hat q$ leave behind. Weighting also cuts single-replicate RMSE in Box B from $0.37$ to $0.19$
(pooled over years), because there the bias dominated the naive estimator's error.

## Bias against $R$ and bandwidth

This exploratory run predates the full ensemble. It uses the first $100$ replicates and
$0.125^\circ\times2.5$ d bins. Within it, the 100 replicates are split into five groups of 20. Each group in turn is the test set, and
$\hat q$ is built from nested subsets of the other 80 ($R=10,20,40,80$) at
$\sigma_s\in\{0.125,0.1875,0.25,0.375,0.5\}^\circ$ and $\sigma_t\in\{3.75,7.5,15\}$ d. By (4.1) the
smoothing term falls with $h$ and the Jensen term falls with $R$. The **two-bandwidth Richardson
correction** $(4\hat H_h-\hat H_{2h})/3$, which doubles both $\sigma_s$ and $\sigma_t$, cancels a
bias term exactly proportional to $h^2$. Its remainders are the $o(h^2)$ smoothing terms, the $O(h)$
boundary terms, and the Jensen term, which it *amplifies*: if that term scales as $(Rh^3)^{-1}$ it
enters the corrected estimator as $\tfrac13(4-\tfrac18)=\tfrac{31}{24}$ of its value at $h$. The
variance also grows by the factor $\operatorname{Var}(4\hat H_h-\hat H_{2h})/9$.
